stem: An infant with diagnosed airway malacia is otherwise well, growing appropriately, and has no worsening symptoms; what is the best overall management approach?

options.text: Treatment is rarely needed; continue follow-up rather than escalating immediately
Start a regular asthma preventer because airway malacia usually behaves like asthma
Use repeated short courses of prednisolone as routine long-term treatment
Arrange bronchoscopy at every review regardless of progress
Start prolonged antibiotics to prevent any future cough

explanation: Treatment is rarely needed for uncomplicated airway malacia. In a thriving infant with no worsening symptoms, the appropriate approach is follow-up and observation rather than immediate escalation.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

rationale: Airway malacia often requires little active treatment when the infant is otherwise well. Escalation is more relevant if symptoms worsen or growth falters.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because uncomplicated airway malacia is usually managed conservatively with follow-up when the infant is well and growing appropriately.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because airway malacia is not routinely managed as asthma, so a preventer is not the standard approach.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because repeated prednisolone is not standard long-term treatment for airway malacia.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because bronchoscopy is not needed at every review when the child is clinically stable.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because prolonged antibiotics are not used to prevent cough in uncomplicated airway malacia.

sourceRefs: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
